Amberford Packaging Reports Production Delay but Retains Financial Headroom

16 October 2026 | Written by Tomas Belwick

Meridian Ratings says a delay to Amberford Packaging’s replacement production line does not currently affect its BBB issuer rating or stable outlook. The company now expects commissioning in February 2027, two months later than planned, following a fault identified during equipment testing at the supplier’s workshop.

The project budget has risen to KRN 81 million from KRN 74 million. Amberford expects to keep its existing line operating until the replacement is ready, allowing it to fulfil contracted orders. The delay will defer expected efficiency savings and add approximately KRN 3 million in temporary maintenance costs.

Meridian’s revised forecast puts peak net debt at 2.9 times operating profit before depreciation, compared with less than 2.8 times previously. Existing liquidity can absorb the additional spending. Further delays, lost orders or substantially higher costs could reduce the headroom supporting the stable outlook and prompt a rating review.

Meridian Downgrades Ostara Homes as Cancellations Increase and Liquidity Weakens

23 October 2026 | Written by Céline Arvane

Meridian Ratings has downgraded Ostara Homes’ long-term issuer rating to BB plus from BBB minus. The outlook is negative. The downgrade follows a sharp increase in cancellations and a reduction in available borrowing facilities, which weaken the company’s ability to carry its growing stock of unsold homes.

Figures supplied on 21 October show that completed but unsold homes reached 289 at September, compared with 246 at August. Cancellations accounted for 27% of gross reservations during September. Cash and undrawn committed facilities fell to KRN 112 million after a lender declined to renew a KRN 40 million facility.

Ostara Homes has suspended new land purchases and plans selective discounts to release cash from finished properties. These steps should help liquidity, but lower selling prices will put further pressure on earnings. Meridian could lower the rating again if available funding falls materially or sales fail to cover construction spending and scheduled debt payments.

Meridian Publishes Updated Criteria for Rating Kestrian District Heating Providers

12 October 2026 | Written by Mara Ternell

Meridian Ratings has published updated criteria for assessing district heating providers in Kestria. The criteria take effect today and apply to new ratings and future reviews. They give more detailed guidance on fuel procurement, seasonal liquidity and the financial effect of delays in recovering costs through customer tariffs.

The update follows a consultation that closed on 18 September. Meridian received nine written responses from rated companies, investors and other market participants. The final text clarifies how analysts assess committed credit facilities and distinguishes fuel already held in storage from purchases covered by future supply contracts.

Meridian has assessed its existing district heating ratings against the revised criteria and identified no immediate rating changes. The update does not alter the rating or outlook on Val-Brume Heating affirmed on 5 October. Individual reviews will continue to consider network condition, customer concentration and each provider’s ability to absorb unexpected costs.

Meridian Affirms Fenmere Commercial Bank as Property Lending Remains Concentrated

19 October 2026 | Written by Elian Voss

Meridian Ratings has affirmed Fenmere Commercial Bank’s BBB long-term issuer rating with a stable outlook. The Saltmarsh-based lender benefits from steady business deposits and adequate capital. Its relatively large exposure to commercial property continues to constrain the rating, particularly lending secured on smaller office buildings.

Commercial property represented 31% of gross loans at the end of September, down from 34% a year earlier. Loans more than 90 days overdue rose to 2.5% from 2.1% over that period. Additional provisions reduced nine-month profit to KRN 47 million, 12% below the comparable period.

The bank’s core capital ratio of 14.2% provides capacity to absorb further losses within Meridian’s base forecast. Deposits increased by 3.1% during the first nine months, supporting liquidity. The stable outlook assumes gradual reductions in property concentration and no sharp deterioration among the bank’s largest borrowers.

Val-Brume Packaging Downgraded to BB+ Following Weaker Cash Generation

By Elise Dorne and Dario Selven
September 24, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has lowered Val-Brume Packaging's senior unsecured bond rating to BB+ from BBB-. The outlook is stable. The producer of cartons and food containers has reported weaker earnings and a larger working capital requirement than Northstar assumed in its previous review.

Operating profit before depreciation fell 22% to KRN 41 million in the year ended July, while debt increased to KRN 205 million. Higher paper input costs and slower customer payments contributed to the deterioration. Debt reached 5.0 times operating profit, compared with 3.6 times a year earlier. The company serves food producers across Kestria from its principal factory in Val-Brume.

Cash of KRN 19 million and an undrawn committed facility of KRN 35 million provide adequate near-term funding. No bond principal is due before 2029. The stable outlook assumes tighter stock control and lower investment spending prevent further debt growth. Another downgrade could follow if cash generation remains negative or available funding falls materially.

By Mara Vellin and Céline Maret
September 18, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has assigned an A- rating to Amberford Water's proposed KRN 230 million senior unsecured bond, with a stable outlook. The company plans to use KRN 150 million to repay existing debt and the remainder to replace ageing mains and pumping equipment. The rating is subject to final documents matching the terms reviewed.

Amberford Water supplies 340,000 households and businesses under a licence that links permitted revenue to operating costs and approved investment. Collections remained strong at 98.6% of billed revenue in the year ended June. Water losses declined to 17.2% from 19.1% following repairs to several older sections of the network.

By Tomas Arven and Céline Maret
September 4, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed Estuary Freight's BBB- senior unsecured bond rating and revised the outlook to negative from stable. The Kestrel Bay cargo handler has KRN 160 million of bonds falling due in February 2027. Discussions with lenders are continuing, but the company has not secured replacement funding.

At 31 July, Estuary Freight held KRN 38 million in unrestricted cash and had KRN 25 million available under committed facilities. Cargo volumes fell 6% in the first seven months of the year, mainly because of lower building material shipments. Northstar estimates debt at 4.4 times annual operating profit before depreciation, against 3.8 times at the end of 2025.

The negative outlook reflects the narrowing time available to refinance. Northstar could lower the rating if funding arrangements remain incomplete or operating performance weakens further. A return to a stable outlook would require sufficient committed funding to repay the bonds and evidence that cargo earnings have steadied.

Meridian Confirms Bracken Freight Rating After Equity Funding Reduces Acquisition Debt

20 October 2026 | Written by Tomas Belwick

Meridian Ratings has confirmed Bracken Freight’s BBB long-term issuer rating with a stable outlook and removed it from review for downgrade. The action follows completion of its KRN 460 million acquisition of Kestrel Bay Harbour Services and confirmation of a larger equity contribution than previously disclosed.

Bracken raised KRN 250 million through an equity issue completed on 19 October and funded the remaining purchase price through its bridge facility. The acquisition completed today. Meridian estimates opening net debt at 2.8 times combined annual operating profit before depreciation, materially below the debt-only case considered on 8 October.

The stable outlook allows for KRN 22 million of integration spending over the next 12 months and assumes no further large acquisitions. Bracken plans to replace the bridge borrowing with longer-term funding within six months. Delayed refinancing or weaker cargo volumes could reduce rating headroom, although current cash generation supports the confirmed rating.

Northstar Opens Consultation on Proposed Corporate Liquidity Assessment Changes

By Nalin Verdan and Dario Selven
September 10, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has opened a consultation on proposed changes to its corporate liquidity methodology. The draft explains how analysts would assess seasonal cash needs, restrictions on moving cash between subsidiaries and borrowing facilities that depend on financial conditions. Written responses are invited until 2 October.

The proposal would require a separate assessment of the weakest three-month cash position within the following year. Current analysis places greater emphasis on the full twelve-month period. The draft also clarifies that an uncommitted overdraft would not count as an assured funding source, even when an issuer has used it regularly.

An initial review of 24 rated Kestrian corporate groups suggests that five could receive weaker liquidity assessments under the draft. This would not automatically change their ratings, which also reflect business strength and debt levels. The existing methodology remains in force during consultation. Northstar will publish its conclusions after reviewing responses and completing further testing.

Kestrian Food Producers Face Narrower Margins as Packaging Costs Rise

By Elise Dorne and Nalin Verdan
August 20, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has revised its outlook for Kestrian packaged food producers to negative from stable. The change reflects higher packaging and distribution costs, together with limited scope to raise selling prices. It is a sector assessment and does not change any individual bond rating.

Across the agency's sample of seven fictional issuers, packaging costs increased by an average of 11% in the first half of 2026, while selling prices rose 3%. Northstar expects the sample's operating margin before depreciation to fall to roughly 9% this year from 10.4% in 2025. Smaller producers supplying shops around Ostara have less purchasing power and face the greatest pressure.

Most rated producers retain adequate cash reserves and have no large bond repayments within twelve months. This should limit immediate rating pressure. The agency will focus on stock levels, customer payment times and whether cost savings protect cash generation. Companies that borrow to fund dividends while margins weaken could face individual rating reviews.

August 17, 2026

SALTMarsh — Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed its BBB rating on Bracken Grid's KRN 420 million senior unsecured bonds. The outlook remains stable. The electricity network operator serves 610,000 connections across Amberford and surrounding districts. Its regulated network income provides a predictable source of cash, although a substantial maintenance programme limits room for additional borrowing.

For the six months ended 30 June, revenue rose 4.2% to KRN 286 million and operating profit before depreciation reached KRN 112 million. Debt stood at 3.7 times annualised operating profit, compared with 3.9 times at December. Available cash and committed borrowing facilities covered the company's next twelve months of scheduled debt payments.

The stable outlook assumes annual capital spending of about KRN 95 million and no material acquisition. Northstar could lower the rating if debt remained above 4.5 times operating profit or network penalties materially reduced cash generation. Corporate Liquidity Consultation Closes with Twelve Responses Under Review

By Nalin Verdan and Céline Maret
October 5, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics received twelve responses to its proposed corporate liquidity methodology changes before the consultation closed on 2 October. Submissions came from rated companies, bond investors and lending firms. Analysts are reviewing the comments alongside additional testing of the proposed three-month cash assessment.

Several respondents supported clearer treatment of restricted cash and uncommitted borrowing. Others asked how the agency would assess seasonal businesses whose lowest cash balance occurs shortly before a predictable collection period. Four submissions requested worked examples showing how financial conditions attached to borrowing facilities would affect available liquidity.

Northstar will consider these points before deciding whether to adopt the changes. No rating or liquidity assessment has changed as a result of the consultation, and the existing methodology remains applicable. By Tomas Arven and Dario Selven
October 15, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has lowered Estuary Freight's senior unsecured bond rating to BB from BBB- and concluded the review opened on 13 October. The outlook is negative. Further information supplied during the review shows that the company has limited readily available funding for its KRN 160 million February 2027 bond repayment.

Of the KRN 25 million previously reported as available under committed facilities, KRN 15 million expires in January 2027. Northstar therefore excludes that amount when assessing resources for the bond maturity. The proposed storage yard sale remains at an early stage, with no agreed buyer or binding timetable. September cargo earnings also fell below management's revised budget.

The downgrade principally reflects weaker refinancing prospects and reduced financial flexibility. The revised liquidity methodology published yesterday also informs the assessment of facility availability. The negative outlook indicates further downside if replacement funding remains unsecured. A stable outlook would require a credible, committed repayment plan and enough cash to continue ordinary operations.

Ostara Rental Housing Outlook Remains Stable Despite Higher Maintenance Spending

By Mara Vellin and Dario Selven
October 8, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has maintained a stable sector outlook for rated rental housing companies operating in Ostara. High occupancy and steady rent collection continue to support earnings, although repairs and borrowing costs are absorbing more cash. The assessment covers four issuers with a combined 28,400 homes.

Average occupancy stood at 97.4% at the end of August, compared with 97.1% a year earlier. Rent arrears remained modest at 1.8% of annual billed rent. Maintenance spending rose 8%, led by roof repairs and heating replacements. Fixed interest rates apply to 76% of the sample's debt, limiting the immediate effect of higher financing costs.

Northstar expects most issuers to fund routine repairs from rental income while keeping development programmes within committed borrowing limits. Ratings could come under pressure where large construction projects coincide with debt maturities. The stable sector outlook assumes occupancy remains above 96% and companies retain enough accessible funding to meet twelve months of planned spending.

Northstar Adopts Revised Liquidity Methodology with Seasonal Cash Guidance

By Nalin Verdan and Céline Maret
October 14, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has published its revised corporate liquidity methodology, effective today. The final document adds a review of the weakest three-month cash position within the following year and clarifies how analysts treat restricted cash, uncommitted borrowing and conditions attached to committed facilities.

Following consultation, the agency has added worked examples for seasonal businesses. Analysts may recognise expected customer receipts when supported by a consistent collection record, but must also test a reasonable delay. Cash held by a subsidiary will count only where it can legally and practically meet the obligations being assessed.

Northstar has also published an anonymised summary of the twelve consultation responses. It will apply the revised methodology to existing corporate ratings over the next three months and to new assignments immediately. Publication itself changes no ratings. Any resulting action will receive a separate release explaining the issuer's circumstances and the role of the revised assessment.

Val-Brume Packaging Rating Affirmed After Investment Spending Is Reduced

By Céline Maret and Dario Selven
October 22, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has affirmed Val-Brume Packaging's BB+ senior unsecured bond rating and stable outlook after the company reduced its investment budget. Management has deferred a second printing line, cutting planned spending for the current financial year to KRN 18 million from KRN 34 million.

The decision preserves cash while the company addresses the working capital pressures behind its September downgrade. Unrestricted cash stood at KRN 22 million at the end of September, with KRN 35 million still available under its committed facility. Early collections from overdue customers helped the improvement, although one month of stronger receipts does not establish a sustained recovery.

Northstar continues to expect debt near 5.0 times annual operating profit before depreciation in the near term. The revised liquidity assessment supports the existing rating because available resources cover projected seasonal needs. An upgrade would require durable earnings recovery and lower debt. Renewed cash outflows, weaker facility access or substantial additional borrowing could lead to another downgrade.

Kestrian Retail Bond Issuers Enter Winter with Uneven Cash Buffers

By Elise Dorne and Nalin Verdan
October 20, 2026

Northstar Credit Analytics has maintained a negative outlook for Kestrian discretionary retailers in its latest sector review. Households are limiting larger purchases, while retailers have already paid for much of their winter stock. The agency expects differences in cash reserves to matter more than modest changes in reported sales.

Among six rated issuers, stock values at the end of September were 9% higher than a year earlier, while sales for the preceding three months rose only 1%. Two chains operating mainly in Saltmarsh and Kestrel Bay increased promotional discounts to clear older goods. Across the sample, average operating margins before depreciation fell to 6.2% from 7.1%.

Four issuers have committed facilities extending beyond their seasonal borrowing peak. The remaining two rely more heavily on cash generated during winter trading. Northstar is testing slower stock sales and delayed supplier credit separately for each company. The sector outlook does not imply that every retailer will be downgraded, and no individual rating changes accompany this report.

Bank introduces clearer monthly statements for variable-rate business loans

Leonie Venn · 13 October 2026

Harrow & Finch Bank has introduced a revised monthly statement layout for variable-rate business loans. Statements issued from today show the reference rate, the borrower’s agreed margin and the number of days charged at each rate in a single interest table.

Where a rate changes during the statement period, separate rows show the balance and calculation for each part of that period. This will help borrowers check interest following the bank’s reference rate reductions in August and September. Fees will continue to appear separately from interest.

New borrower support team offers earlier repayment difficulty reviews

Devran Holt · 22 October 2026

Harrow & Finch Bank has established a dedicated borrower support team for business customers facing repayment difficulties. The five-person team is based in Saltmarsh and accepts referrals from relationship managers across Kestria. Customers can also ask their usual lending contact for a support review.

Half-year sales rise as GreenBasket reports lower operating profit

30 September 2026Daniel Rooke, Corporate Affairs

GreenBasket Supermarkets, Kestria's largest supermarket chain by store count, reported revenue of KRN 6.42 billion for the 26 weeks ended 30 August 2026, up 4.1 per cent on the comparable period. Sales at stores open for at least a year rose 2.7 per cent.

Operating profit fell from KRN 206 million to KRN 193 million. Higher wage and refrigeration maintenance costs outweighed savings in distribution. GreenBasket invested KRN 118 million in stores, equipment and delivery vehicles during the period, including the Eastmere opening in Amberford. It ended the half year with 215 stores.

Finance director Anika Pell said customers were buying more own-label groceries and making smaller, more frequent trips. Own-label products accounted for 58 per cent of grocery units sold, compared with 55 per cent a year earlier. Online orders represented 9.4 per cent of revenue, up from 8.7 per cent in the comparable period.

GreenBasket recalls selected oat biscuits after incorrect allergen labelling

9 September 2026Sofia Merrow, Corporate Affairs

GreenBasket Supermarkets is recalling its 250-gram Honeyfield Oat Biscuits with batch code HB0902 and a best-before date of 18 February 2027. The affected packs contain milk, which is missing from the allergen statement. They are unsuitable for people with a milk allergy.

The biscuits were sold in 87 GreenBasket stores across Kestria between 3 and 8 September. Customers with a milk allergy should not eat them. Anyone who bought an affected pack can return it to any GreenBasket store for a full refund without a receipt. Other batch codes are not included in this recall.

GreenBasket identified the error during a packaging check yesterday and removed the affected stock from sale that evening. Recall notices are displayed in the relevant stores and on the customer website. Product safety manager Orla Venn said the company had received no reports of illness linked to the affected batch.

Small suppliers receive shorter payment terms under new purchasing policy

26 August 2026Idris Weller, Corporate Affairs

GreenBasket Supermarkets has introduced payment terms of 14 calendar days for qualifying small suppliers, replacing its previous standard of 30 days. The policy applies to new purchase orders issued from today. A total of 186 existing suppliers meet the published eligibility rules.

Suppliers qualify if their annual turnover is below KRN 12 million and they employ fewer than 50 people. Payment is measured from receipt of a valid invoice after delivery. GreenBasket has removed the administration charge previously applied when suppliers requested payment before their contractual due date.

Procurement director Nella Corven said smaller producers often paid wages and bought materials well before receiving money for their goods. A dedicated accounts team in Saltmarsh now handles questions about the scheme. Suppliers can check eligibility and invoice status through their existing account, or request the same information by telephone.

GreenBasket Supermarkets has completed a KRN 3.8 million refurbishment of its Harbour Steps store in Kestrel Bay. The shop remained open throughout the eight-week project. GreenBasket Supermarkets opened its Eastmere store in Amberford today, bringing its network to 215 shops across Kestria. The 1,420-square-metre store employs 46 people, including 31 colleagues recruited locally. It has eight staffed checkouts, a bakery and a collection desk for online orders.

The store stocks bread, dairy products and vegetables from 23 suppliers based within 80 kilometres of Amberford. Shelf labels identify where these products come from. Customers can buy loose portions of 34 fruit and vegetable lines, with weighing scales beside the produce section.

Store manager Tessa Brindle said the layout had been tested with residents before opening. Changes included wider gaps between promotional displays and lower shelving near the entrance. The store also has step-free access, two accessible checkout lanes and a covered seating area beside the main doors.

Ostara depot changes cut damaged produce deliveries by nearly a quarter

8 October 2026Idris Weller, Corporate Affairs

GreenBasket Supermarkets has reduced damaged fruit and vegetable deliveries from its Ostara depot by 24 per cent following changes to packing and loading. The result compares damage recorded per thousand crates during July to September with the same three months of 2025.

The depot supplies 68 stores and handles about 410,000 produce crates each month. Changes included shallower crates for soft fruit, separate loading positions for heavier root vegetables and temperature checks at each loading bay. GreenBasket spent KRN 1.7 million on equipment and training for the work.

Depot manager Brenna Holt said staff had recorded where damage occurred before changing handling routines. The measured reduction represents approximately 7,800 fewer damaged crates over the quarter. Produce rejected by stores remains subject to the same quality checks, and items suitable for sale are assessed separately from stock that must be discarded.

GreenBasket publishes clearer rules for supplier deductions and invoice disputes

15 October 2026Idris Weller, Corporate Affairs

GreenBasket Supermarkets has introduced a supplier code covering invoice disputes, delivery deductions and changes to orders. Effective today, the code requires buyers to provide written reasons and supporting records before making a deduction. It applies to all goods suppliers across the company's 216 stores.

Suppliers now have a single route for challenging deductions through a commercial review team separate from their usual buyer. The code sets a ten-working-day deadline for an initial written response. Undisputed invoice amounts remain payable under the supplier's agreed terms while a challenge is examined.

Procurement director Nella Corven said discussions with 73 suppliers had highlighted inconsistent explanations for shortages and damaged deliveries. The new code also requires written agreement before suppliers are charged for a promotion. It does not change the 14-day payment terms for eligible small businesses, whose first payment report was published yesterday.

First payment report shows progress for GreenBasket small suppliers

14 October 2026Daniel Rooke, Corporate Affairs

GreenBasket Supermarkets has published its first payment report since introducing 14-day terms for qualifying small suppliers on 26 August. Of the 2,460 invoices due under the scheme by 30 September, 96.2 per cent were paid within the agreed period. Average payment time was 12.6 calendar days.

The report covers invoices with a combined value of KRN 18.4 million. Ninety-four were paid late, most following internal approval delays. All 94 had been settled by 9 October. GreenBasket has added a daily review of approaching payment deadlines and assigned a named contact to each participating supplier.

Finance director Anika Pell said the late payments fell short of the company's commitment. The report lists disputed invoices separately and does not count them as paid on time. Seventeen invoices remained in dispute at the reporting date, with reasons supplied to the businesses concerned. The figures cover the small-supplier scheme rather than GreenBasket's entire supplier base.

28 Sep 2026

Lumen Home Retail will shorten opening hours at its Kestrel Bay Harbour Lane branch while contractors replace part of the roof. From 5 to 16 October, the store will open from 9 am to 6 pm each day. Its usual opening hours are 7 am to 9 pm.

The repair budget is KRN 640,000. Grocery shopping, the pharmacy counter and customer toilets will remain available during the temporary opening hours.

Online collection customers with bookings outside the revised hours will be contacted directly and offered another slot or free home delivery. Staff will retain their contracted pay, with some shifts moved to stock preparation and nearby delivery operations. Lumen expects normal hours to resume on 17 October, subject to the final building inspection.

Vegetable growers join longer supply programme for Kestrian produce

25 Sep 2026

Lumen Home Retail has agreed a two-year vegetable supply programme with Reedplain Growers, a group of 18 farms outside Amberford. The programme covers potatoes, carrots, onions and cabbages sold in Lumen stores across Kestria. The first deliveries under the new terms begin on 1 October.

The agreement sets minimum purchase volumes for each crop and provides a quarterly review of growing, packing and transport costs. Lumen expects to buy about 6,400 tonnes during the first year. Orders will include smaller and unevenly shaped vegetables for its lower-priced cooking bags, provided they meet the same freshness requirements as other produce.

Participating farms will receive payment within 14 days of an accepted delivery. Lumen will share a rolling 12-week forecast, updated each week, to help growers plan harvesting and labour. Produce labels will identify the growing area, while store teams will receive guidance on storage temperatures and handling to reduce damage between delivery and sale.

Lumen agrees new credit facility to support planned store investment

23 Sep 2026

Lumen Home Retail has signed a KRN 120 million revolving credit facility with Brackenmere Commercial Bank and Ternfold Lending. The facility matures in September 2030 and replaces a KRN 90 million agreement that was due to expire next year. It provides funds that Lumen can draw and repay as needed.

At signing, KRN 28 million was drawn under the new agreement to repay the outstanding balance on the previous facility. The remaining capacity is available for seasonal stock purchases and planned investment in stores and distribution equipment. No shares were issued as part of the financing.

Finance director Sella Morven said the agreement gave Lumen greater certainty over funding while retaining room for quieter trading periods. Interest is charged at a variable reference rate plus an agreed margin. The facility includes quarterly borrowing and interest-cover tests. Lumen met those requirements at signing and has not changed its full-year investment budget of KRN 34 million.

Lumen Home Retail has signed a three-year supply agreement with Hearthmere Baking, a family-owned producer based in Ostara. From 21 September, the bakery will supply bread and rolls to 14 Lumen stores, extending an existing arrangement covering six branches. The agreement is worth an estimated KRN 7.2 million over its term.

Existing bakery suppliers will continue serving Lumen stores outside the expanded delivery area.

Lumen outlines Saltmarsh depot upgrade ahead of winter trading

23 Oct 2026

Lumen Home Retail will invest KRN 4.6 million in new sorting equipment and additional chilled holding space at its Saltmarsh distribution depot. The upgrade will add 320 chilled pallet spaces and replace two ageing conveyor sections used for household goods. Lumen expects the changes to reduce manual handling and give stores more flexibility when ordering fresh food. Ostara tray plant cuts trim waste through tooling changes

By Tobin Merrow · September 29, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging's Ostara plant has reduced trim waste on two chilled-food tray lines following changes to cutting tools and sheet positioning. Across eight weeks of measured production, trim represented 13.1 per cent of material fed into the lines, down from 16.4 per cent during the preceding eight weeks.

The comparison covers the same four tray designs and excludes trial runs. Staff adjusted the spacing between tray shapes and replaced worn cutting edges. The plant used 18 tonnes less sheet material than it would have used at the earlier trim rate for the recorded volume.

Tray dimensions, sealing surfaces and approved material specifications are unchanged. Clean trim from these lines is separated for controlled reprocessing, subject to the requirements of each product specification. Corvel is reporting the reduction as a material efficiency measure; it has not calculated a carbon saving from the work.

Energy surcharge rises as packaging production costs increase

By Ellis Dacre · September 22, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has increased its energy surcharge from KRN 42 to KRN 58 per tonne for goods dispatched from today. The rate covers cartons, trays and films made at its three production sites. Base prices remain unchanged under this adjustment.

Purchased energy costs have risen further since the surcharge was introduced on 31 August. The latest four weeks of production records show an average energy cost increase of KRN 67 per tonne against the company's May reference level. Corvel is absorbing the difference between that increase and the surcharge.

An order containing 2.5 tonnes of packaging now carries a surcharge of KRN 145 before tax. The dispatch date determines the applicable rate, including for orders placed earlier. Invoice weight details remain available by product line. Customers with a fixed-price agreement should refer to its surcharge terms or contact their account manager for an explanation.

Corvel updates carton prices following higher board costs

By Ellis Dacre · September 30, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has increased base prices for newly quoted folding cartons by an average of 3.4 per cent from today. Individual changes range from 2.1 to 4.6 per cent, depending on board grade, carton weight and print requirements. Confirmed orders retain their agreed base prices.

The adjustment follows higher delivered board costs recorded during August and September. It applies to cartons produced at Amberford and does not change the base prices of trays or films. The energy surcharge remains separate at KRN 58 per tonne and is calculated using dispatch weight.

Revised quotations show the base price and estimated surcharge separately so customers can compare the full cost at a stated order quantity. Existing written quotations remain valid until their stated expiry dates. Account teams can review board grades or order sizes with customers, although any specification change still requires approval before production.

Corvel introduces separate energy surcharge on food packaging orders

By Ellis Dacre · August 31, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has introduced an energy surcharge of KRN 42 per tonne on cartons, trays and films dispatched from today. The charge applies to domestic orders across Kestria and appears as a separate invoice line. Base product prices are unchanged.

The surcharge reflects higher electricity and process heating costs at the company's Amberford, Ostara and Kestrel Bay plants. Corvel's combined energy cost per tonne of finished packaging was 14 per cent higher in August than in May, despite lower consumption on several production lines.

For an order weighing 2.5 tonnes, the surcharge is KRN 105 before tax. It does not apply to goods dispatched before today, even where the invoice is issued later. Customer statements show the dispatch weight used in the calculation, and account teams have received a common worksheet to explain the charge and resolve weight queries.

Corvel publishes clearer weight details on packaging invoices

By Nadia Pell · September 1, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has updated its invoices to show the net packaging weight used to calculate its energy surcharge. The revised layout lists product weight, surcharge rate and surcharge value together. Pallets, outer wrapping and returnable transport frames are excluded from the calculation.

The change follows questions received when the KRN 42 per tonne surcharge took effect yesterday. For mixed deliveries, each product line carries its own weight and charge. Where an order is split between dispatches, the invoice includes only the quantity sent in that delivery.

Customers can also obtain the same weight breakdown from their account contact without requesting a replacement invoice. Corvel has checked the revised layout against 30 sample orders covering cartons, trays and films. The checks found no change to the amount charged; the update makes the calculation easier to follow and compare with delivery records.

Corvel Packaging adds carton capacity at Amberford plant

By Mara Venn · August 25, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has brought a second carton folding line into service at its Amberford plant. The line adds capacity for 1.8 million food cartons a month, increasing the site's monthly folding capacity to 7.2 million units. It handles sleeves and folding cartons used for chilled meals, bakery products and dry foods.

Installation and production trials cost KRN 4.6 million. During acceptance checks, staff ran six carton sizes and measured fold accuracy, glue application and print alignment. Twelve employees have completed training on the equipment, including operators transferred from the site's older finishing area.

The additional capacity addresses demand from customers in Amberford and Saltmarsh. Orders remain subject to the usual checks on board availability and artwork approval. Customers with approved carton designs can ask their account contact to review order quantities against the expanded production schedule.

Corvel publishes evidence sheets for selected carton recycling claims

By Tobin Merrow · October 9, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has issued evidence sheets for 18 uncoated carton specifications supplied from Amberford. Each sheet identifies the board grade, coatings, inks and adhesives covered by the assessment. It also explains the conditions attached to the company's recycling statements.

The sheets draw on fibre separation tests and checks of collection guidance available in Saltmarsh, Amberford and Val-Brume. Results apply only to the listed specifications. Cartons with film windows, barrier layers or heavy food contamination require separate consideration and are outside the scope of this release.

Customers can request a sheet using their carton specification number. The documents support packaging decisions but do not establish that every local collection service accepts a carton. Corvel advises customers to check disposal wording against the collection arrangements serving their buyers. No new recycling claim has been added to customer artwork as part of this work.

Corvel adds recycled content option for selected food trays

By Tobin Merrow · October 15, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has added a tray material containing 35 per cent recycled plastic by weight to its Ostara product range. The option is available for two clear chilled-food tray sizes. It uses recycled material from a controlled process assessed for the specified food contact conditions.

Qualification checks covered material traceability, tray strength, sealing and migration under chilled storage conditions. The trays are approved for the listed chilled foods and temperatures in their technical sheets. They are not approved for oven use. Customers must confirm that their intended food and filling process match those conditions.

Kestrel Bay film line returns after planned maintenance

By Mara Venn · October 8, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has returned its second film line at Kestrel Bay to normal production following a four-day maintenance shutdown. Work included replacing heater controls, checking winding equipment and servicing the cooling system. The line produces sealing films for prepared-food trays.

Operators completed restart checks on three film thicknesses before releasing production. Tests covered thickness variation, roll tension and seal performance against approved tray samples. All three trial batches met their existing specifications. The work has not changed the materials used or the approved uses of the films.

Corvel supplied scheduled orders from stock built before the shutdown, and no confirmed delivery dates were missed. Both film lines at Kestrel Bay are now operating. Customers receiving material from the restarted line can find the production batch reference on each roll label and on the accompanying quality record.

Corvel opens French language customer desk in Val-Brume

By Nadia Pell · October 5, 2026
Share: LinkedIn X Email

Corvel Packaging has opened a French language customer desk in Val-Brume to support food producers in Kestria's French-speaking region. Three customer service staff now handle order enquiries, delivery updates and invoice questions from the office. The desk operates on weekdays from 08:30 to 17:00 local time.

Customers can request quotations, specification summaries and surcharge explanations in French. Technical approval remains with the production site responsible for the packaging. The desk uses the same order records as Corvel's Saltmarsh team, allowing staff to check quantities and dispatch information without creating a separate customer account.

The office supports customers buying cartons, trays and films; it does not hold stock or receive returned goods. During its internal service trial, staff handled 64 sample enquiries covering all three product groups. Customers already assigned an account manager retain that contact and can use the new desk for routine order support.

Rain Raises Drying Demand At Ostara Grain Receiving Site

AMBERFORD, Kestria, Sept. 16, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Rain around Ostara has increased the proportion of wheat deliveries requiring drying at Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative's local receiving site. Of the 61 wheat loads sampled during the past two days, 24 exceeded the standard moisture limit of 14 per cent. Accepted wet grain is being stored separately.

The site's dryer has processed 460 tonnes since the rain began. Members are being given a moisture reading and an estimated drying charge before unloading. The charge depends on the moisture removed and is separate from the purchase price shown on the member's grain agreement.

Receiving staff have reduced the number of wet-grain bookings to match drying capacity. Dry wheat and oat bookings remain available, subject to storage space. Members should report their latest moisture reading when arranging a delivery and should not mix damp grain with a dry load to meet the acceptance limit.

Kestrel Bay Loading Repairs Restore Normal Grain Dispatch Capacity

OSTARA, Kestria, Oct. 6, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative has restored normal dispatch capacity at its Kestrel Bay store after replacing a worn bearing in the grain loading conveyor. The conveyor returned to service on 5 October following an inspection and an unloaded test. Grain receiving continued while the equipment was unavailable.

The interruption delayed nine customer collections carrying a combined 270 tonnes of wheat and oats. Six have now been completed, and revised collection times have been agreed for the remaining three. No grain was damaged, and the affected conveyor did not require any stored stock to be discarded.

The loading line is again operating at its normal rate of up to 90 tonnes an hour, subject to vehicle changes and sampling. Customers should use the collection time shown on their latest dispatch confirmation. Drivers arriving early must wait in the marked parking area until called to the loading point.

Stock Check Confirms Grain Records Across Four Storage Sites

KESTREL BAY, Kestria, Oct. 22, 2026 /KestriaWire/ -- Prairie Gold Grain Co-operative has completed its autumn stock check at Amberford, Ostara, Kestrel Bay and Val-Brume. Measured stocks at the close of 21 October totalled 121,460 tonnes of wheat and 34,280 tonnes of oats. The figures include grain already allocated to customers but awaiting collection.

Staff compared bin measurements with receiving tickets, dispatch weights and recorded cleaning losses. The combined difference between measured grain and stock records was 0.08 per cent, within the co-operative's internal tolerance of 0.20 per cent. All four sites completed checks, and no unexplained difference required a customer allocation to be changed.

Routine temperature readings also found no storage parcel above the co-operative's action threshold of 20 degrees. Store teams continue to check grain condition and record aeration work. Customers requesting available volumes should contact the sales desk, as total physical stock includes committed grain and parcels held for further preparation.

Bramble Foods announces October price changes for selected snacks

By Tobin Vale

20 August 2026

Bramble Foods has notified retail customers of price increases averaging 2.5% across selected biscuits and savoury snacks, effective from 1 October 2026. The changes apply to wholesale list prices in Kestria. Standard sliced bread and plain bread rolls are excluded from this announcement.

The company said higher costs for edible oils, cocoa ingredients and flexible packaging had continued through the summer. Savings from purchasing and factory improvements have absorbed part of those increases. Individual product changes will vary, and retailers will decide the prices paid by shoppers.

17 August 2026

Bramble Foods, the listed Kestrian bakery and snacks company, today reported revenue of KRN 428.6 million for the six months ended 30 June 2026, up 6.4% on the same period last year. Third quarter sales rise as bakery demand remains steady

By Mara Fenwick

19 October 2026

Bramble Foods recorded revenue of KRN 219.4 million for the three months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of 4.8% compared with the same quarter last year. Revenue for the first nine months reached KRN 648.0 million. Third-quarter sales volumes grew by 1.3%, supported by steady bread demand and higher cracker sales.

Trading remained strongest in Saltmarsh and Amberford, while orders from smaller shops were more variable. The new oat cracker range began shipping near the quarter end and made only a small contribution. Wholesale price changes introduced on 1 October had no effect on the reported quarter.

The board's full-year operating profit expectations remain unchanged. Regular production on Amberford's new packing line began today, with performance monitoring under way. The proposed Hearthmere Bakery acquisition has received competition clearance but has not yet completed. Its trading is therefore excluded from these figures, and completion remains expected by the end of October.

Oakhill Bakeries Group has introduced a single delivery charge for small shop orders across its existing delivery network in Kestria. Orders below KRN 240 now carry a KRN 12 charge. Orders at or above that value receive delivery without a separate fee.

Oakhill Bakeries Group has begun consultation with the 31 employees at its Ostara bakery over a proposal to close the site. No final decision has been made. The bakery produces sandwich rolls and plain buns in a building with limited space for modern equipment.

The site has a daily capacity of 14 tonnes, although average output over the past six months was eight tonnes. Maintenance and energy costs per tonne have risen as production has fallen. The company is examining whether work can be transferred to its other bakeries.

Employees have received written details of the proposal and can attend individual meetings during paid working time. Oakhill is considering alternatives submitted by staff, including changes to shifts and products. Posted: Friday, October 16, 2026
Posted by: Mara Denholt

Oakhill Bakeries Group reduced bread production waste to 2.8 per cent of baked weight in September, down from 3.6 per cent in June. The comparison covers Amberford, Saltmarsh and Ostara, which operated during both months. It excludes the new Kestrel Bay bakery.

The measure includes misshapen loaves, products damaged during packing and bread rejected during quality checks. It does not include unsold goods returned by shops, which Oakhill records separately. Production waste across the three sites fell from 54 tonnes in June to 43 tonnes in September.

Teams adjusted dough portion settings, improved checks at shift changes and replaced worn guides on two packing lines. Operations director Brenna Halewick said these small changes reduced avoidable losses without relaxing product standards. Site teams review the figures weekly, using weighing records and production totals to identify where further checks are needed.

News release

Gas network ruling disallows unsupported maintenance costs

Published: 30 September 2026

The Kestria Energy Board has disallowed KRN 1.8 million of maintenance costs claimed by the Saltmarsh gas network operator. The ruling follows a review of expenditure for the year ended 30 June. The operator did not provide sufficient work records to support costs assigned to 23 maintenance jobs.

The disputed amount forms part of a KRN 41.6 million maintenance claim. The Board accepted KRN 39.8 million after checking invoices, inspection records and staff time entries. The disallowed costs cannot be recovered through regulated network charges. This decision does not alter the tariff currently shown on customer bills.

The ruling concerns evidence supporting expenditure. It makes no finding that the maintenance itself was unnecessary or that the network is unsafe. The operator must keep clearer records linking each charge to completed work. A summary of the assessment explains the evidence requirements and lists the categories of costs that were excluded.

Supply restrictions on the East Ostara industrial gas branch have been lifted following repairs to a pressure regulator. News release

Board clarifies billing rules following household tariff reduction

Published: 17 September 2026

The Kestria Energy Board has issued billing guidance following the household electricity standing charge reduction on 15 September. The guidance addresses questions received from customers and suppliers about bills covering days on both sides of the change. It does not introduce another tariff change.

For a bill covering 1 to 30 September, suppliers must charge 14 days at KRN 0.84 and 16 days at KRN 0.79. The standing charge for that period is therefore KRN 24.40. Electricity used during the period remains subject to the unchanged unit rate of KRN 0.246 per kilowatt hour.

Customers using advance credit meters are also entitled to the lower standing charge from 15 September. Where a meter update has taken longer, suppliers must credit the difference. The Board has asked suppliers to keep records of these adjustments so its billing team can check that customers receive the full reduction.

News release

Board publishes annual review of electricity network charges

Published: 20 August 2026

The Kestria Energy Board has published its annual review of electricity network charges. The review covers the cost of carrying power to homes and businesses across Kestria. It records KRN 184 million in allowed network revenue for the year ended 30 June, against actual spending of KRN 179 million.

Most of the difference came from delayed cable replacement in Amberford and lower maintenance costs around Saltmarsh. The Board has required network operators to explain how the unspent allowance is recorded in their accounts. Operators cannot treat money allowed for unfinished work as an unrestricted surplus.

The review does not change customer tariffs. It also reports that average electricity interruptions fell from 74 minutes to 68 minutes per customer over the year. Rural districts west of Ostara remained above that average, at 112 minutes. The full review includes separate spending and service tables for each network area.

Electricity tariff decision reduces standard household standing charge

News release

Amberford electricity connection delays prompt formal improvement notice

Published: 6 October 2026

The Kestria Energy Board has issued a formal improvement notice to the Amberford electricity network operator after an audit found repeated delays in providing connection quotations. Of 160 complete applications examined, 47 had not received a quotation within the required 15 working days.

The applications covered small shops, workshops and housing developments. The longest recorded wait was 38 working days. The operator attributed the backlog to vacancies and incomplete internal handovers. The Board found that these problems did not remove its obligation to meet the published service standard.

The notice requires weekly reporting of outstanding quotations and a named contact for every affected applicant. It also requires the operator to separate applications awaiting customer information from those delayed within its own teams. The notice imposes no financial penalty. Applicants can ask the operator for a written explanation of their case and use the Board's complaints route if it remains unresolved.

News release

Board approves lower overnight network charge for industry

Published: 16 October 2026

The Kestria Energy Board has approved a lower overnight electricity network charge for eligible industrial connections in Kestrel Bay. From today, the charge for electricity carried between midnight and 05:00 is KRN 0.018 per kilowatt hour, down from KRN 0.023. Other network rates remain unchanged.

The decision covers 38 connections with meters that record consumption in half-hour periods. Network evidence showed spare capacity during the overnight window and lower costs for carrying additional demand at those times. The Board accepted the proposed reduction after checking the operator's demand records and allocation of costs.

A qualifying site using 100,000 kilowatt hours entirely within the overnight window pays KRN 500 less in network charges for that consumption. This is only one part of its electricity bill. Energy supply prices, capacity charges and other applicable items are separate. Suppliers must identify the revised network rate clearly in their billing calculations.

News release

Quarterly report records fewer unresolved energy billing complaints

Published: 20 October 2026

The Kestria Energy Board has published its complaints report for July to September. It received 642 electricity and gas complaints during the quarter, compared with 689 in the preceding quarter. There were 118 unresolved cases at the end of September, down from 151 at the end of June.

Billing accounted for 61 per cent of new complaints. The most common issues were estimated consumption, delayed corrections and unclear account balances. Connection delays accounted for a further 17 per cent. The figures cover cases brought to the Board after customers had first raised the matter with their supplier or network operator.

The median time taken to close a case was 19 working days, compared with 23 in the preceding quarter. The Board cautions that a closed case does not always mean a complaint was upheld. Its tables distinguish corrections, explanations, withdrawn cases and formal findings so readers can see how complaints were resolved.

Strong winds interrupt crane operations across container terminal

Ellis Corven 3 Sep 2026

Container crane operations at the Port of Kestrel Bay were suspended between 05:40 and 11:10 today after wind speeds exceeded the terminal's operating limit. Instruments on the quay recorded gusts of 78 kilometres per hour. Cranes were secured, and staff were withdrawn from exposed working areas.

Three vessels experienced delays, including one using the reduced working area at Berth Four. By 14:00, all operational cranes had returned to service following safety checks. Shipping agents have received revised departure estimates based on the remaining cargo moves for each vessel.

Freight gates remained open, but some drivers waited longer while container lifts were paused. The authority cancelled waiting charges for vehicles held inside the terminal during the suspension. No injuries, dropped containers or damage to lifting equipment were reported. Repair crews at Berth Four also stopped exposed work during the strongest winds.

News release

Meter checks find errors in industrial electricity bills

Published: 13 October 2026

A Kestria Energy Board audit has identified incorrect meter multipliers on nine industrial electricity accounts in Kestrel Bay. A multiplier converts the meter's recorded reading into the amount of electricity supplied. Using the wrong value can produce an incorrect bill even when the meter itself works properly.

Seven accounts were overcharged by a combined KRN 286,400 over periods ranging from four to eleven months. Two accounts were undercharged by a combined KRN 31,700. The supplier has accepted the findings and issued corrected account statements. All nine affected businesses have been contacted individually.

The Board has required repayment of the overcharges and a check of the supplier's remaining industrial meter settings. Any recovery of undercharges remains subject to the applicable billing rules and complaint rights. The audit found an account configuration problem, with no evidence of a fault in the physical meters or an interruption to electricity supply.

North freight gate reopens after overnight equipment fault

Ellis Corven 26 Aug 2026

The north freight gate at the Port of Kestrel Bay reopened at 09:20 today after a fault in its vehicle recognition equipment. The gate closed at 02:15. Freight traffic used the south entrance while technicians replaced a damaged power unit and checked the control system.

A total of 186 lorry bookings were affected. Drivers with valid bookings were admitted through the south gate without making a second booking, and the authority waived missed-slot charges linked to the closure. The longest recorded queue was 38 vehicles shortly before 07:00. No injuries or damage to cargo were reported.

Both freight entrances are now operating normally. Drivers whose booking records still show a missed visit can ask the gate office to correct the entry, quoting their vehicle registration and booking number. The fault did not affect rail movements, vessel operations or access to the empty-container yard.

September figures show shorter queues at freight gates

Mara Venn 5 Oct 2026

Average lorry turnaround time at the Port of Kestrel Bay fell to 39 minutes in September, compared with 43 minutes in July. The monthly figure covers 31,480 completed visits and includes time spent waiting inside the terminal. Visits cancelled before arrival are excluded.

The port handled 82,900 standard container units during September. This was 2.4 per cent above the same month last year, despite the wind stoppage on 3 September and the reduced working length at Berth Four. Rail accounted for 29 per cent of containers leaving the port by land.

Gate staff recorded fewer arrivals without bookings after hauliers began receiving an additional booking reminder in August. Unbooked arrivals fell from 412 in August to 267 in September. The authority asks drivers to check the container release status before travelling, as a gate booking alone does not confirm that cargo is ready for collection.

Container volumes rise as inland rail services expand

Mara Venn 21 Aug 2026

The Port of Kestrel Bay handled 84,600 standard container units in July, an increase of 6.2 per cent compared with July last year. Food products, household goods and machine parts accounted for most of the growth. The figures count a forty-foot container as two standard units.

Rail carried 28 per cent of containers leaving the port by land, up from 24 per cent a year earlier. Two additional weekly services between the port and Amberford began operating in June. The inland terminal at Amberford now receives eight port trains each week.

Average lorry turnaround time was 43 minutes during July, measured from entry at the freight gate to departure. This was four minutes shorter than in June. The authority publishes these figures to help hauliers and cargo owners compare port performance. Empty containers and loaded containers are included in the gate measure.

Rail signalling fault delays inland container departures today

Ellis Corven 13 Oct 2026

A signalling fault at Reedbank Junction interrupted freight rail access to the Port of Kestrel Bay today. The junction operator stopped movements at 06:25 after a track detection circuit failed. Three outbound trains carrying a combined 144 containers were held in the port rail yard.

One train was bound for Amberford and two for the Saltmarsh inland terminal. The line reopened at 13:40 following replacement of the faulty component and a test movement. The first delayed train left the port at 14:05. No containers were transferred to road transport during the closure.

Rail customers received revised departure details through their booking contacts. Containers held on the affected trains have been exempted from additional port storage charges caused by the interruption. Vessel loading and unloading continued throughout the incident, and freight gates remained open. The fault occurred outside the port boundary and did not affect the terminal's internal rail equipment.

Port clears delayed vessel queue after fog restrictions

Ellis Corven 22 Oct 2026

The Port of Kestrel Bay cleared its delayed vessel queue at 15:30 today after dense fog restricted harbour movements overnight. Visibility at the outer entrance fell below 200 metres, and vessel movements were suspended from 23:10 yesterday until 07:45 today. Five arriving vessels were held at the designated anchorage.

Harbour staff resumed movements after visibility improved and patrol crews checked the entrance channel. Departing vessels moved first where this released an occupied berth. Two container vessels, two general cargo ships and one coastal tanker then entered under revised arrival slots agreed with their agents.

Cargo work continued on vessels already alongside during the restriction. Freight gates and rail services operated normally, although collection times changed for some containers aboard the delayed arrivals. Customers can check release status through their usual account record. No collisions, groundings or injuries were reported during the fog restriction or the clearance of the queue.

New bilingual freight guidance supports Val-Brume cargo customers

Tomas Bellwick 19 Oct 2026

The Port of Kestrel Bay has published freight collection guidance in English and French following requests from cargo customers in Val-Brume. The guidance covers gate bookings, container release checks, driver identification and the documents needed to collect goods through an appointed haulier.

Customers with billing addresses in the French-speaking region accounted for 12 per cent of loaded import collections during the first nine months of this year. The port's customer team reviewed 160 enquiries from those customers when preparing the guidance. Missing release references and uncertainty about collection authority were the most common problems.

Both language versions are available from the freight desk and in the customer account area. Printed copies carry the same numbered steps so staff and drivers can refer to the same instruction. The guidance explains existing procedures and introduces no additional documents or charges. Customers can request help from a French-speaking member of the customer team.

Packaging levy revision removes duplicate reporting for manufacturers

Media centre · Mara Vennick
17 September

The Food Manufacturers Federation of Kestria has welcomed a revised packaging levy proposal published today by the Ministry of Revenue. The revision provides for one reporting return and removes a provision that could have counted some packaging twice.

The proposed rate remains KRN 0.18 per kilogram for the materials covered. The ministry has also added examples showing how manufacturers should record packaging purchased through wholesalers and packaging transferred between factories.

Mara Vennick, policy director, said: “These changes address a practical problem raised in our submission. Businesses can now assess the proposal with a clearer understanding of what they would need to report.”

The federation continues to seek clarification on reusable transport containers and the treatment of returned goods. It has asked members to submit examples with weights and purchase records. The levy remains a proposal, and the federation advises businesses to distinguish the draft requirements from their existing reporting duties.

Summer survey shows steady orders but tighter margins

Media centre · Tomas Bellan
1 September

Food manufacturers reported steady summer orders but continued pressure on margins, according to a survey published today by the Food Manufacturers Federation of Kestria. The survey received responses from 84 businesses employing 12,600 people.

Forty-six per cent said their order volumes were broadly unchanged from the previous three months. Thirty-one per cent reported an increase and 23 per cent a decline. Responses were collected between 10 and 24 August.

Packaging and maintenance were the most frequently reported sources of higher costs. Fifty-eight per cent of respondents said their operating margin had narrowed, while 37 per cent had postponed at least one planned equipment purchase.

Tomas Bellan, research manager, said: “Stable orders are welcome, but they do not mean every business is comfortable. Manufacturers in Amberford and Kestrel Bay described particular difficulty finding affordable replacement parts.” The federation cautioned that the voluntary survey represents participating members rather than the entire sector.

Elise Marvaux, technical affairs manager, said: “A bakery in Val-Brume should be able to reach the same answer as a sauce maker in Ostara. Clear examples would reduce mistakes and unnecessary calls for advice.”

The federation has submitted six worked examples and requested guidance in both Kestrian and French. It also recommends allowing businesses to use existing compliant packaging stocks when the change concerns presentation alone, provided all required consumer information remains accurate and legible.

Sector wage agreement approved by employers and union members

Media centre · Devran Pell
23 October

The new food manufacturing sector wage agreement has been approved by participating employers and members of the Food Production Workers Union. The Food Manufacturers Federation of Kestria confirmed the result after both approval processes concluded.

Fifty-six of the 63 participating employers voted in favour. The union reported support from 78 per cent of members who voted. The agreement takes effect on 1 November and covers approximately 9,400 employees.

The adult production minimum will rise to KRN 14.85 an hour, shift allowances will increase by 4 per cent and covered employees will receive eight hours of paid job-related training each year. The signed terms retain existing protections for higher contractual rates.

Devran Pell, employment relations manager, said: “Approval gives payroll teams and employees certainty about the new terms. Our immediate priority is helping employers apply them correctly.” The federation has issued an implementation checklist covering payroll changes, staff notices and training records.

Trading resumes after morning interruption to order entry

Notice No. 2026/362 · Category: Trading hours

Date of issue: 08.10.2026 · Effective: 15.10.2026

Trading in wheat, oat and rapeseed futures resumed at 10:05 today after an interruption to the exchange's order entry service. Ostara Commodities Exchange suspended matching at 09:12 when monitoring identified delays in order acknowledgements. A ten-minute period for members to review and cancel orders preceded the reopening.

Trades completed before the suspension remain valid. Orders that had been accepted and remained unfilled were retained with their original priority. Messages that did not receive an acceptance acknowledgement were not added to the order book. Members were asked to reconcile their records against the exchange's order and trade reports before entering replacement instructions.

Technical staff traced the interruption to a fault in a message queue and moved the service to reserve equipment. The regular 16:30 closing time remains in place. Clearing and warehouse reporting services continued to operate during the interruption. The exchange is reviewing system records and member reports to establish why the fault was not resolved automatically.

Exchange completes review of order entry service interruption

Notice No. 2026/376 · Category: Margins

Date of issue: 15.10.2026 · Effective: 22.10.2026

Ostara Commodities Exchange has completed its review of the order entry interruption on 8 October. The review found that a software fault caused an internal message queue to stop releasing acknowledgements promptly. Automatic recovery did not start because the monitoring check measured connection availability without checking whether messages were progressing through the queue.

The exchange has added a separate check for message progress and tested the transfer to reserve equipment under simulated delays. It has also revised the procedure used by technical staff to confirm that order entry is ready to reopen. These changes are in operation. The review found no alteration to completed trade records.

Reconciliation with clearing members is complete, and no unresolved differences remain between accepted orders and the exchange's records for the affected period. Members can request their own message logs through the support service. The exchange has published a technical incident note setting out the interruption times, the cause and the checks applied before trading resumed.

Rapeseed delivery rules clarify sampling and retained records

Notice No. 2026/369 · Category: Contracts

Date of issue: 14.10.2026 · Effective: 28.10.2026

Ostara Commodities Exchange has issued a clarification of the sampling procedure for rapeseed delivered against its futures contracts. From today, delivery inspection records must state the sampling time, lot reference and seal numbers for retained samples. The clarification applies at every warehouse approved to handle exchange rapeseed deliveries.

Inspectors must prepare three sealed samples from each delivery lot: one for the seller, one for the buyer and one held by the warehouse. The warehouse sample must be retained for 45 calendar days after ownership transfers. Where a quality dispute remains open, it must be retained until the exchange confirms that the case is closed.

The maximum moisture content remains 9 per cent, and the maximum foreign matter allowance remains 2 per cent. Contract size and approved delivery locations are unchanged. Members can obtain the revised inspection form in English or French. Forms already completed for transferred lots remain valid; warehouses are not required to reopen completed deliveries solely to add the new record fields.

Exchange introduces calendar spread orders for wheat futures

Notice No. 2026/390 · Category: Trading hours

Date of issue: 23.10.2026 · Effective: 30.10.2026

Ostara Commodities Exchange has introduced calendar spread orders for wheat futures. Members can now submit a single order to buy one listed wheat delivery month and sell another in equal quantities. The service is available during the regular 08:30 to 16:30 session and uses the same contract specifications as outright wheat trading.

Spread prices represent the price of the later delivery month minus the price of the earlier month, quoted in KRN per tonne. The minimum price movement is KRN 0.25 per tonne, equivalent to KRN 5 for a spread covering one 20-tonne contract in each month. Both sides execute together, removing the need to submit two separate outright orders.

Completed spreads create a separate futures position in each delivery month. Existing delivery obligations and position limits continue to apply to those positions. The exchange's published margin schedule determines the collateral required, including any eligible offset between months. Members can access worked examples and test messages through the document and test services. Oat and rapeseed order types are unchanged.

Annual report records faster action on unpaid pension contributions

Written by Mara Ellwick

The Pensions Oversight Authority's annual report, published today, records KRN 6.8 million in overdue employer contributions recovered following its intervention during the year ended 31 March 2026. The payments reached 73 workplace pension plans covering 18,420 members. Recoveries totalled KRN 5.1 million in the previous reporting year.

The median time from opening a contribution case to securing payment fell from 47 to 34 working days. The Authority issued 29 financial penalties and required improvements to record keeping at 61 plans. These figures cover completed cases; they do not include money still being pursued at the year end.

Operating expenditure was KRN 24.6 million against a budget of KRN 25.2 million. The report includes audited accounts, service measures and a breakdown of complaints about the Authority. Priorities for the current year include earlier checks on missed payments and clearer guidance for employers running smaller workplace plans.

Consultation opens on clearer recovery plans for underfunded pensions

Written by Tomas Vennick

The Pensions Oversight Authority is seeking views on proposed changes to the information employers and trustees provide when a workplace pension plan is underfunded. The consultation opens today and closes on 30 October. The proposals concern plans that promise members a set retirement income.

Under the proposals, recovery plans would explain why the payment schedule is affordable, what would happen if trading weakened and how trustees would monitor progress. A standard summary would show annual contributions in KRN alongside the expected funding shortfall. The Authority is also asking whether smaller plans need a shorter reporting form.

No funding rules change today. Existing recovery plans and payment schedules remain in force. Employers, trustees, advisers and members can respond through the Authority's consultation service or by post to its Saltmarsh office. An accompanying paper includes worked examples for a manufacturer, a transport business and a community services employer.

Val-Brume pension clinic offers support with annual returns

Written by Celia Bramwell

Trustees and employers in the Val-Brume area can now book free appointments at a pension reporting clinic on 8 October. Staff from the Pensions Oversight Authority will explain common annual return requirements and help visitors identify information missing from their records. Appointments will be available in French and English.

The clinic will take place at the Authority's Val-Brume office, with 36 appointments lasting 25 minutes each. Visitors should bring their plan registration number and a list of questions. They should not bring members' identity documents, bank details or individual medical records. Telephone appointments are available for those unable to attend.

The service follows a review of 94 returns from plans administered in the region. The most frequent errors concerned membership totals and changes to trustee contact details. Staff can explain reporting requirements but cannot complete returns for applicants or provide investment advice. Booking closes on 5 October, unless all appointments are filled earlier.

Amberford employer fined after repeated delays to pension contributions

Written by Leila Corven

The Pensions Oversight Authority has fined Amberford employer Brindle Quay Components KRN 42,000 after it repeatedly paid workplace pension contributions late. The company missed payment deadlines in seven months between September 2025 and April 2026. The delays affected 286 members of its workplace pension plan.

The employer has now paid the outstanding KRN 193,400, together with KRN 8,760 to compensate the plan for lost investment income. The fine is separate from those payments and must be paid by the company. It cannot be taken from pension assets or charged to members.

The Authority issued its final decision after considering the company's response to an earlier notice. The company has 28 days to appeal. Trustees have been asked to check contributions each month and report further delays. Members do not need to submit individual claims to receive the compensation within the plan.

Workplace pension funding improves in second quarter review

Written by Mara Ellwick

The Pensions Oversight Authority estimates that workplace pension plans promising a set retirement income held assets equal to 104 per cent of their liabilities at the end of June. This compares with 102 per cent at the end of March. The review covers 842 plans across Kestria, with combined assets of KRN 186 billion.

The improvement mainly reflects higher investment income and employer contributions. Funding remains uneven: 176 plans held less than the estimated amount needed to meet their promises. A national average does not show whether an individual plan can pay every benefit when it falls due.

Employers and trustees should continue making scheduled payments and reviewing their funding assumptions. The figures are estimates based on quarterly returns, rather than full valuations of every plan. The Authority has published regional tables, including separate results for Saltmarsh, Kestrel Bay, Ostara, Amberford and Val-Brume.

Employers given clearer steps for reporting late pension payments

Written by Tomas Vennick

The Pensions Oversight Authority has published guidance explaining how employers and trustees should report late workplace pension contributions. It includes examples covering payroll errors, missing payment references and repeated delays. The guidance applies to reports made from today and does not change the legal payment deadlines.

Trustees should record when a payment was due, the amount outstanding and the steps taken to recover it. Where a report is required, it should distinguish money deducted from staff pay from contributions owed by the employer. Employers should give trustees a named contact who can resolve payment queries.

During the first six months of 2026, the Authority received 318 reports involving late payments. Of these, 241 were resolved within 20 working days of the initial report. The new guidance includes a reporting checklist and sample payment record, with versions available in English and French.
